question: The decarbonisation of road transport and the transition to zero-emission vehicles – such as battery electric cars, vans, trucks, and buses – depend on a full suite of enabling conditions. A dense network of charging and refilling stations, tailored to different vehicle segments, is essential but not the only requirement.

Achieving the ambitious CO₂-reduction targets for 2030 requires a minimum infrastructure network to be operational by then. Under the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation1 (AFIR), Member States must ensure infrastructure deployment and regularly monitor progress. 1.

Which Member States have submitted their draft national policy frameworks for alternative fuel market development and infrastructure deployment, as Article 14(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 required them to do by 31 December 2024?
What measures will the Commission take to enforce compliance with this obligation?

Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 of 13 September 2023 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure (OJ L 234, 22.9.2023, pp. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1804/oj (http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1804/oj)).
answer: The following Member States have submitted their draft national policy frameworks (NPF) for alternative fuel market development and infrastructure deployment, as per Article 14(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 (1) by 1 December 2025: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Finland, France, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovenia, Sweden.

The Commission sent a reminder in May 2025 to Member States who had not submitted their draft NPF by then. In September 2025, the Commission has opened pre-infringement dialogues with the Member States that had not submitted their draft NPF by September 2025.
